title: Mother of man shot to death by cop drops RCMP lawsuit
article: The mother of a 22-year-old British Columbia mill worker shot in the back of the head by an RCMP officer said she is abandoning her lawsuit against the force.

At a joint media conference with the RCMP on Wednesday in Vancouver, Linda Bush said the decision was motivated by changes police officials have made to their handling of in-custody deaths and the reforms under consideration.
Bush said she did not want to relive the 'anger and despair' a civil case would have rekindled and that the cost of continuing the legal battle given B.C.'s user-pay regime was too heavy.
'(The court costs) put it out of reach for ordinary people,' she said.
Bush estimated well over $130,000 raised through donations across the country had already been spent on fighting for justice in her son's death.
'I know many people, including some who are very close to me, will be very disappointed with the decision,' she said.
'I do, however need to make the decision after considering what makes the most sense... Nothing we can do will give Ian's life back to him, so the only thing we truly want is not within our reach.'
Bush said she felt much more 'comfortable' with the Mounties now than she did 4 1/2 years ago and couldn't say whether that was from 'forgiveness or maybe a form of acceptance.'
Ian Bush was killed in October 2005 during a struggle in the Houston RCMP detachment after he was arrested with an open beer outside the northern B.C. town's arena during a hockey game.
The officer was never charged.

Chief Superintendent Craig Callens, the B.C. deputy criminal operations officer who accompanied Bush at Wednesday's news conference, said she had given officials 'significant' help in refining their policies.

'On behalf of the RCMP, I would like to thank you for the time and energy you have dedicated to seeing this process through. I can only imagine how emotionally difficult this has been for you and your family.'
Bush said that while she was not happy giving up her fight, she believed she is achieving 'justice for all of us, not necessarily for Ian.'
But she added that it was important to move forward and very important for effective civilian oversight of the force to be established.
In November, B.C. New Democrat MP Nathan Cullen introduced a private member's bill that proposed the creation of an independent watchdog to probe cases of deaths in RCMP custody.
He said the bill would create a civilian watchdog modelled on Ontario's Special Investigations Unit, which handles any Ontario Provincial Police's in-custody deaths.
His initiative was sparked by Bush's death, which happened in his riding.
In February, RCMP Commissioner William Elliott announced the officers would no longer investigate other officers in cases involving serious injury or death of suspects.
As a part of the interim policy, the Mounties refer cases to outside police forces, or provincial or federal review agencies.

In cases where it is not possible to call in outside investigators, the new policy ensures that officers are screened for conflict of interest and that the investigating officer outranks the officer being probed.

But this decision has little effect in B.C., which, unlike Ontario and Alberta, does not have an independent civilian-led agency with the power to investigate police-involved deaths or serious injuries.

The provincial government is thought to be considering such a force but officials are waiting for the final report of the inquiry into the October 2008 death of Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski, who was Tasered by police at the Vancouver International Airport.
At the moment, the RCMP asks municipal departments to investigate police-involved fatalities or serious injuries.

Last year, the B.C. Association of Chiefs of Police unanimously called for the creation of a civilian-led unit for the 'investigation of incidents involving police that have resulted in serious injury or death to any person as well as sensitive allegations of police misconduct.'

Retired B.C. Supreme Court judge William Davies, who conducted the inquiry into the death of Frank Paul, who froze after being in Vancouver police custody, recommended the creation of an SIU-type unit.

And Paul Kennedy, the former head of the Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP, released a report last summer recommending that the RCMP refer investigations to outside police forces to ensure independence. He also pushed for more civilian involvement in probes involving death, serious injury and sex assault.
